title: LLM chat snapshot: streaming params & retry resilience - Meridian Retail intro
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation focusing on streaming behavior, parameter choices (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and resilient retry/idempotency patterns. Customer is evaluating a pilot for chat-based product recommendations with tight latency targets and PII constraints.
topics: Console hints for batching & Optimize recommendations
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-19 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Xander Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Redwood Product), Priya Narang (Meridian Lead Engineer), Tom Keller (Meridian CTO), Sophie Lin (Meridian PM), Daniel Wu (Meridian DevOps)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick host demo + Q&A; follow-ups: security pack + sample request patterns + small perf pilot.

00:00 Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from redwood, super excited to run through a quick hosted chat snapshot and show streaming + params + retry patterns. is this still a good time for you?
00:10 Priya: yes, thanks ava. we've got about 40ish minutes. tom and sophie and danial on — daniel joined a little late. our main ask is how we can get low latency for personalized product suggestions and what the retry story is. also we need to understand data handling for PII.
00:26 Ava: great — we'll cover that. xander will take the runtime bits, i'll show the console and example payloads, and maya will call out optimize suggestions we recommend for cost/latency.
00:37 Xander: quick qual — what's your current inference approach? are you probing open models or running a managed endpoint?
00:44 Tom: we have an in-house light endpoint backed by a mid-size model on k8s, but it's inconsistent; spikes kill latency. we're looking at hosted first then maybe dedicated if traffic justifies it. timeline: pilot in 6 weeks, production in 3-4 months if results are good.
01:02 Xander: cool. important to know — for hosted you get streaming responses that reduce perceived latency; we also support continuous batching and prefix caching.
01:12 Sophie: what do you mean by prefix caching? we've seen K-V cache references but not sure how it helps.
01:18 Xander: right — K-V cache (sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in some docs) lets the runtime reuse hidden states during multi-turn chats so later tokens generate much faster. it's especially handy if user sessions repeat similar context.
01:34 Ava: i'll share a sample request in the console in a sec. maya, can you call out parameter tradeoffs?
01:39 Maya: sure — temperature and top_p are the usual knobs: higher temperature adds diversity but can increase token length unpredictability; top_p controls nucleus sampling. for determinism we suggest low temp + beam-like configs or use sampling with controlled top_p. also watch max_tokens and stop sequences to bound cost.
01:58 Priya: how does streaming change billing? do we pay per token regardless?
02:03 Ava: yes, billing is per output token; streaming just changes delivery, not unit economics. but Optimize can recommend quantization/model variants per workload to reduce per-token cost.
02:15 Xander: now demoing a console session, showing a chatgen request. here's a sample body: model: 'redwood/llm-v2', stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 150, stop: ["\n\n"] — notice streaming chunk frames appear as they generate.
02:36 (screen share audio) Xander: you'll see partial deltas, so client UI can render tokens as they arrive which feels instantaneous vs waiting for full response. also we provide chunk ids so you can detect gaps.
02:48 Daniel: if a chunk fails midstream, what's best practice? do we re-request that turn or resume?
02:55 Xander: good question. common pattern: use an idempotency key for the request and a short retry with backoff. because streams are incremental, if connection breaks you can re-issue the same request with same idempotency token and the server will return consistent output, or we support resume ranges in some SDKs — but resume is more complicated. recommended: small exponential backoff, 3 attempts, then fallback to a lighter model variant for degraded experience.
03:22 Sophie: can you show a retry header in a sample response?
03:26 Ava: sure — in the network tab you'll see x-redwood-retry-count and x-redwood-server-model fields; plus an overall request-id. we also surface a suggestion in the console for backoff intervals.
03:36 Tom: SLA questions — what's typical p95 latency on hosted for a 150-token generation?
03:43 Xander: depends on model and region; for curated open models we see p95 around 220–450ms for short responses in our benchmarks for v2 sized models. longer sequences push that. we'll include a performance sheet in follow-up.
03:57 Priya: security: we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and KMS for keys. also possible data residency in eu.
04:07 Ava: we have SOC2 and ISO attestation docs; SAML SSO with SCIM and fine-grained RBAC. for private deployments we can offer private control plane or VPC peering. KMS integrations available, including HSM for key wraps. we'll attach the security pack.
04:26 Priya: okay good. what about retention — is transient data kept?
04:31 Ava: hosted defaults to short retention for metadata but actual customer data retention policies can be configured — for regulated workloads we recommend Redwood Private or encryption-at-rest + KMS and a zero-retention policy.
04:40 Sophie: maya, any Optimize tips for a pilot with cost cap?
04:43 Maya: yes — run a small traffic profile and we send quantization suggestions, batch sizes, and a model routing policy: e.g., route 80% to a 4-bit quantized variant for recommendations and 20% to a full precision variant for final checkout confirmations. that keeps cost down while preserving quality.
05:03 Tom: demo time please.
05:06 Xander: jumping into a live request. I'll run a few turns so you can see streaming tokens and a simulated connection drop.
05:12 (live audio, keyboard)
05:15 Xander: sending request — streaming on — client receives partial frame: "Hi! How can I help you find items today?" then a second frame with suggestions.
05:28 (simulated drop)
05:30 Xander: okay i forced a disconnect. client automatically retried with idempotency token and got the full transcript back — you can see the SDK retries are silent by default but we log them.
05:40 Priya: were there duplicate charges when you retried?
05:44 Ava: no — idempotency prevents duplicate billing for the same request id within a short TTL. the server dedupes. billing tokens are tied to final accepted response.
05:53 Daniel: what about long polls for websockets vs http streaming? we prefer websockets for persistent low latency.
05:59 Xander: websockets are supported and give lower reconnection overhead; http/2 streaming works too. choose based on client environment. we often recommend websockets for mobile app chat flows.
06:12 Sophie: question on rate limits — how do burst policies look?
06:16 Ava: hosted has tiered rate limits; you can request higher burst windows for pilot. Dedicated gives predictable throughput with reserved GPU pools. we can model your traffic to recommend capacity.
06:28 Tom: are function/tool calls supported for catalog lookups?
06:31 Maya: yes, we support structured tool calls and can return JSON blobs for downstream calls. you can use our function schema to avoid hallucinations for product attributes.
06:41 Priya: demoed the console logs — i see an odd tokenization mismatch where product sku turned into two tokens weirdly. is tokenization something to watch?
06:48 Xander: yes tokenization can affect cost; we provide tokenizer tools in the SDK and console to pre-encode so you can estimate tokens. also Optimize can flag high-token patterns in prompts.
06:57 Sophie: any common misconfigurations we should avoid?
06:59 Xander: common ones: setting temperature high for deterministic tasks, very large max_tokens for short responses, forgetting stop sequences, and not using idempotency keys for repeatable user actions.
07:12 Priya: can you show how to set an idempotency key in a sample curl?
07:16 Ava: yep — header: X-Idempotency-Key: "meridian-session-12345-turn-1" and include the same body. sdk examples do this for you.
07:26 Tom: what happens if a user edits their last message and we re-send with different context?
07:29 Xander: then it's a new request and should have a new idempotency key; reusing the old key with a changed body leads to a conflict. we return a 409 conflict for body mismatch.
07:41 Sophie: latency vs cost question — how do you strike that in defaults?
07:45 Maya: defaults favor higher quality; for strict latency budgets we recommend lower sampling cost models, shorter max_tokens, and enable prefix caching + batching where appropriate. we can run simulations with your traces to produce a cost/latency curve.
08:02 Priya: timeline recap: pilot in 6 weeks — what do you need from us?
08:07 Ava: access to a 24–48‑hour sample traffic trace, a few prompt templates, and a security contact. we'll provision a pilot org, recommend model/quant settings, and run a small perf test.
08:18 (middle portion — deeper Q&A, 8–30 minutes)
08:25 Tom: deep dive — how are kernel selections affecting long sequence throughput?
08:29 Xander: our runtime picks kernels per architecture and sequence length distribution; we auto-switch fast attention kernels for causal short contexts and memory-optimized kernels for long contexts — that reduces token latency.
08:43 Priya: any quirks with quantized models and generation quality?
08:46 Maya: 4-bit quant often holds up well for recommendation style prompts, but you might see small drops on nuance. Optimize runs evals against test prompts to quantify regression.
09:01 Daniel: logging level — what do we get in audit logs?
09:05 Ava: request metadata (id, model, region, timestamp), but by default we don't store user message text unless enabled for debugging; for compliance we can enable encrypted logs with access controls.
09:15 Priya: can we do eu-only region?
09:18 Ava: yes — hosted eu regions and private deployments can satisfy residency. we'll mark that in follow-up.
09:25 Sophie: demoed console's Optimize tab — shows batching suggestions, model swap ideas, and a projected $/1M tokens cost.
09:34 Maya: note the per-route throttle settings and autoscaling policy that you can tweak in console; it shows token and latency breakouts.
09:42 Priya: edge case: repeated quick retries by mobile clients causing burst — any guard rails?
09:47 Xander: we recommend client-side jitter + exponential backoff and server-side per-client throttles; Console exposes per-token budgets so you can cap clients.
09:58 (later portion — wrap-up, 38–48 minutes)
38:10 Ava: recap — we'll send security pack, performance benchmark sheet, and sample SDK snippets with idempotency examples. can we lock a follow-up in two weeks for pilot kickoff?
38:24 Tom: yes, two weeks works.
38:27 Priya: action: we'll prepare traffic trace and list of prompt templates.
38:31 Ava: perfect. i'll email the next steps and link to a short checklist in the console.
38:38 Sophie: one last quick — competitors: we are also evaluating other vendors; can you provide a quick feature vs cost snapshot?
38:45 Ava: yes we'll include a simple comparison and highlight where hosting + dedicated + private differ on cost and control.
39:00 Xander: final note — if you want to stress test we can run a small paid benchmark with your traces to show p95/p99 numbers end-to-end.
39:09 Tom: good. thanks everyone, this was helpful.
39:13 (meeting ends)
